title: How a circle of friends in Nairobi helps fund surgery around the world
summary: A WhatsApp group, a shared pool, and a lot of love. For years, Bidii Circle has looked out for one another in Nairobi. Now they're choosing patients around the world to support.
body_markdown:
A few times a year, a group of friends in Nairobi, Kenya, gets together in person. The rest of the time, they stay close through a busy WhatsApp group. They call themselves[Bidii Circle](https://watsi.org/company/bidii-circle?ref=watsi.org) .


*In Swahili, bidii means effort or diligence.*


Over the years, these friends have built their own way of looking after each other. Members pay into a shared pool that anyone in the group can borrow from when they need it. They also set money aside to support one another's families through life's big moments.


It's a simple idea: when life happens, nobody in the circle has to face it alone.


### A tradition of pulling together


In Kenya, this kind of collective care runs deep. One expression of it is *harambee* , a Swahili word meaning "all pull together." It describes a community rallying around a person or family, often to help with medical bills, weddings, funerals, and other moments too big for one household to carry.


[Jane Ngige-Muturi](https://watsi.org/meet-jane) is a member of Bidii Circle and a Watsi Program Advisor based in Nairobi. She sees a clear line between harambee and the way her friends give.


> "Being part of a community that cares for one another is a real gift. We're even more grateful for the opportunity to help pass that generosity along and play a small part in supporting someone’s health and recovery," shared Jane.


For years, that care stayed within the circle. Then the friends began asking a new question: what would it look like to share some of it with people they'd never met?


### Choosing the patient who calls out to you


The circle decided to give through Watsi, where they could read about individual patients waiting for surgery and choose who to support.


Members didn't limit themselves to Kenya. Each person read through patient stories from around the world and picked someone whose situation stayed with them.


> As one member put it, it was about choosing "the patient who called out to your heart."


As of November 2026, Bidii Circle has helped fund care for[23 patients](https://watsi.org/company/bidii-circle?ref=watsi.org) , contributing $675 together. The patients come from different countries and backgrounds. Each one is a person, and a family, who needed surgery they couldn't otherwise afford.


Bidii Circle's impact around the world with Watsi


### What giving together makes possible


Bidii Circle didn't need a formal organization or an elaborate plan to get started. They brought what they already had — friends who trust each other, a habit of showing up, and a willingness to try something new.


That's what makes giving circles work. They give people a place to talk about what matters to them, learn from one another, decide together, and see what their combined gifts can do. It's the same spirit behind[Watsi's college chapters](https://watsi.org/paying-it-forward/) , and behind the everyday donors who[shared why they give](https://watsi.org/who-gives/) .


For Bidii, Watsi has been their first experience of giving beyond their own community. The same care they've practiced with each other for years now reaches families in places they've never been.


A small circle can reach much further than itself.


**Thank you, Bidii Circle, for bringing your generosity, and your joy, to the Watsi community.**


*If you and your friends have been talking about*[giving together](https://watsi.org/campaigns?ref=watsi.org) *, you can start the same way Bidii did.*[Browse the patients raising funds today](https://watsi.org/?ref=watsi.org) *and see who calls out to you.*
